text: Time to write your first JOIN. This is the moment everything from Chapter 3's first lesson pays off — we're going to combine rows from two different tables into one result.

P dot name, p dot list price, s-o-d dot order quantity. From Production dot Product, aliased as p. Inner join Sales dot SalesOrderDetail, aliased as s-o-d. On p dot ProductID equals s-o-d dot ProductID. That ON clause is a predicate, exactly like the ones from Chapter 2 — it decides which rows from each table actually get paired together. And notice those short aliases, p and s-o-d — once two tables share a column name like ProductID, you have to say which table's ProductID you mean, and aliases make that fast to type.

Here's the single most important thing to understand about INNER JOIN: it only returns matches. A product that's never been ordered has no row in SalesOrderDetail to pair with — so it simply doesn't appear in this result at all. Anything unmatched, on either side, just disappears.

And everything from Chapter 2 still works exactly the same after a join. WHERE, ORDER BY — they just operate on the combined, already-joined rows. Where color equals red, order by order quantity descending — filtering and sorting, right on top of a join.

ON decides the match, aliases keep it readable, and INNER JOIN keeps only what matched on both sides. Next lesson: LEFT JOIN, for when you actually want to keep those unmatched rows instead of losing them. See you there.
